+  "purpose": "Define the complete, compilable shape and exact observable behavior of monokl's query language -- query/mod.rs's public re-exports, query/lexer.rs's Token enum and Lexer, query/parser.rs's Modifier enum, ParsedTerm struct, parse() function and content_to_term() helper, and query/plan.rs's QueryPlan struct -- per docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Section 5 (lines 643-897), so a developer implementing or testing the query pipeline never has to guess a token boundary, an escape rule, a modifier's fate through a specific input, or which terms search_patterns() actually surfaces. Unlike every prior track this project has spec'd, this cluster is dominated by algorithmic behavior, not type shape: Lexer.next_token()'s dispatch rules, read_quoted()'s escape handling, and parse()'s multi-token lookahead logic each admit precise, non-obvious, and in one case (the \"+regex:foo\" input) already-documented failure behavior that only a careful trace of the actual control flow reveals. This track traces that control flow exactly, including docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md finding #8's precise claim -- that \"+regex:foo\" doesn't merely lose its Required modifier as the code's own comment states, but discards the regex semantics entirely, degrading to an Optional, escaped-literal match on the bare word \"foo\" -- by tracing parser.rs's exact token-by-token handling of that input, not by restating the finding's own summary.",

+  "scope": "query/mod.rs's public re-export surface (Modifier, ParsedTerm, parse from parser; QueryPlan from plan); query/lexer.rs's Token enum (6 variants) and Lexer<'a> struct (2 private fields, zero derives, 2 public methods, 6 private helper methods); query/parser.rs's Modifier enum (3 variants), ParsedTerm struct (3 fields), the parse() function's complete token-dispatch logic including its LIMIT=64 term cap and empty-input early return, and the content_to_term() helper's exact Word/QuotedString/RegexPrefix/other handling; and query/plan.rs's QueryPlan struct (4 fields) and its from_terms/is_empty/search_patterns methods -- all verbatim per 01-core-architecture.md:643-897. It locks: Token's structural shape and Lexer's total lack of any derive; the exact dispatch order and byte-consumption behavior of Lexer::next_token() for each of Plus/Minus/quote/regex-prefix/word/Eof; read_word()'s greedy-until-whitespace consumption (so '+'/'-'/'\"' are only special at token-start, never mid-word); read_quoted()'s single-escape (\\\") rule and its silent tolerance of an unterminated quoted string; the precise, traced consequence of \"+regex:foo\" and bare \"regex:\" inputs, including cases where a regex: prefix produces zero terms; parse()'s term-count cap and its exact interaction with the already-locked MonoklError::TooManyTerms variant (SPEC-001 AC-008); that regex pattern validity is never checked at this layer; and QueryPlan's exact term-to-category partitioning and search_patterns()'s required-then-scored (never excluded) output ordering.",
+    "tokens.rs's tokenize()/tokenize_source() functions (docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Section 6) -- a separate, later track (Track 7 per .claude/plans/ACTIVE.md).",

+    "text_search.rs's search_files() and the rank/ module's consumption of QueryPlan and its search_patterns() output (docs/spec/01-core-architecture.md Sections 7-8) -- separate, later tracks (Tracks 8-9).",

+    "MonoklError's own enum shape, Display text, or any variant other than confirming TooManyTerms's already-locked construction site here -- already locked by SPEC-001; this track states only that parse() constructs MonoklError::TooManyTerms { count: terms.len(), limit: 64 } at one specific point, per SPEC-001 AC-008's existing Display-text lock.",

+    "Whether an is_regex: true term's pattern string is ever validated as a syntactically valid regex, and the specific, already-documented inconsistency between two later pipeline stages' handling of an invalid one (docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #7, cited as context) -- this track states only that parser.rs itself performs no such validation; resolving or even fully describing finding #7's downstream inconsistency is a later track's responsibility.",

+    "Whether QueryPlan's is_empty() should instead check required/scored specifically rather than total term count, or whether an exclusion-only query (docs/spec/07-edge-cases-and-failure-modes.md Part 1 finding #21, cited as context) should surface a diagnostic -- this track documents QueryPlan's current, verbatim is_empty() semantics precisely; deciding whether to change them is a behavioral decision for whichever track implements the search command's own query-plan consumption."
+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:673-675. Constructs a Lexer positioned at the start of input (pos: 0). Never fails.",

+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:736-752. Advances the lexer past leading whitespace, then returns exactly one Token, mutating the lexer's internal position. Never returns a Result; malformed input (e.g. an unterminated quoted string) produces a Token, never an error. See AC-004 through AC-007.",

+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:778-837. Tokenizes and interprets the full input string into a Vec<ParsedTerm>, applying the modifier/regex-prefix/term-count-limit logic in AC-009 through AC-015. Returns Ok(Vec::new()) for whitespace-only input, Err(MonoklError::TooManyTerms) if more than 64 terms result, Ok(terms) otherwise -- never any other error variant.",
+        "MonoklError::TooManyTerms { count, limit: 64 } when the parsed term count exceeds 64 (SPEC-001 AC-008)."

+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:873-884. Partitions terms by modifier into required/excluded/scored index vectors, each preserving the relative order of the matching terms' original positions in terms. Never fails; an empty terms vec produces a QueryPlan with all four fields empty.",

+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:886. Returns self.terms.is_empty() -- true only when the total term count (across all three categories combined) is zero. See AC-018 for the consequence on exclusion-only queries.",

+      "description": "01-core-architecture.md:888-892. Returns pattern strings for required-category terms first, then scored-category terms, each in its own preserved relative order; excluded-category terms never appear in this method's output. See AC-019.",

+      "criterion": "Token (01-core-architecture.md:657-665) compiles with #[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)] -- no Eq, no Copy, no Serialize/Deserialize -- and exactly 6 variants in this order: Plus (unit), Minus (unit), RegexPrefix (unit), QuotedString(String) (1-tuple), Word(String) (1-tuple), Eof (unit). Token has no JSON representation whatsoever: it never appears in any serde-derived struct's field, and attempting to use it where Serialize/Deserialize is required would be a compile-time E0277 failure naming Token specifically, the same class of consequence SPEC-006 AC-015 and SPEC-008 AC-002 establish for LineHit and TsconfigMode.",

+      "criterion": "Lexer<'a> (01-core-architecture.md:667-670) carries NO derive attribute of any kind -- not Debug, not Clone, not PartialEq, nothing -- making it the first type this project has locked with zero derives at all; every other type with a reduced derive set (LineHit, TsconfigMode, WorkspaceOptions) still carries at least #[derive(Debug, Clone)]. Its 2 fields, input: &'a str and pos: usize, are both private (no pub keyword on either), so no code outside query/lexer.rs's own impl block can read or construct a Lexer's fields directly -- the only way to obtain one is Lexer::new.",

+      "criterion": "Lexer's public API surface is exactly the 2 methods listed in api_surface -- new and next_token. The 6 other methods defined in its impl block (remaining, peek, advance, skip_whitespace, read_word, read_quoted; 01-core-architecture.md:677-734) are all private (no pub keyword), and are implementation details of next_token's own logic, not part of Lexer's public contract -- a caller outside query/lexer.rs cannot call any of them directly, and their exact behavior is described here (AC-005, AC-006) only insofar as it determines next_token's own observable output, not as an independently-callable contract.",

+      "criterion": "Lexer::next_token() (01-core-architecture.md:736-752) always calls skip_whitespace() first, unconditionally consuming every leading ASCII-whitespace byte before inspecting the next character. It then dispatches on the first non-whitespace character in this exact order: no character remaining (EOF) produces Token::Eof; '+' consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Plus, regardless of what character (if any) follows; '-' likewise consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Minus; '\"' consumes exactly 1 byte (the opening quote) and then delegates to read_quoted() to produce Token::QuotedString(...) (AC-006); any other character first checks whether the remaining input starts with the exact, case-sensitive 6-byte literal \"regex:\" -- if so, consumes exactly those 6 bytes and produces Token::RegexPrefix, with no lookahead at what follows; otherwise, delegates to read_word() to produce Token::Word(...) (AC-005). This dispatch order means '+', '-', and '\"' are checked before the \"regex:\" prefix check, which is in turn checked before falling back to a generic word.",

+      "criterion": "read_word() (01-core-architecture.md:701-714) greedily consumes every character from the current position up to (but not including) the next ASCII-whitespace character or EOF, with no other stopping condition -- '+', '-', '\"', and the literal substring \"regex:\" are ordinary characters to read_word and do not terminate it early when they occur anywhere other than the very first character of a token (which next_token's own dispatch, AC-004, has already special-cased before read_word is ever called). Consequence: the input \"foo+bar\" tokenizes as a single Token::Word(\"foo+bar\") -- the '+' does not split it into separate Plus and Word tokens, because next_token only inspects the FIRST character of a token to decide dispatch, and read_word does not stop at internal '+' characters once it has been invoked.",

+      "criterion": "read_quoted() (01-core-architecture.md:716-734) is called after next_token has already consumed the opening '\"'; it repeatedly calls advance() (which consumes and returns the next character) and, on each iteration: a closing '\"' or EOF (None) ends the loop, with the closing quote itself (if present) consumed but not appended to the result string, and with NO error raised in either case -- an unterminated quoted string (EOF reached before any closing '\"') returns whatever characters were accumulated so far as a normal, successful QuotedString value, indistinguishable from a properly-terminated one by its return type alone. A backslash character triggers a peek (not a consuming advance) at the next character: if that peeked character is exactly '\"', the closing-quote lookalike is consumed (an additional pos += 1) and a single literal '\"' is appended to the result -- this is the ONLY recognized escape sequence. For any other peeked character (including another backslash, or no character at all if input ends immediately after the initial backslash), the backslash itself is appended literally to the result and the peeked character (if any) is left unconsumed, to be processed as an ordinary character on read_quoted's next loop iteration. Any character other than a closing quote or a backslash is appended to the result as-is. Concrete examples below describe each input as an explicit sequence of characters, spelling out any backslash or quote character in words rather than relying on a backtick-quoted code span to convey a precise character count, since a code span cannot by itself distinguish \"one backslash character\" from \"a source-level escape sequence representing one backslash character\" -- the same ambiguity that made an earlier draft of this criterion self-contradictory. Example 1: input is the 5 characters quote, f, o, o, quote (no backslashes) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: f, o, o. Example 2: input is the 6 characters quote, a, backslash, quote, b, quote (a backslash immediately followed by a quote character) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: a, quote, b -- the escaped quote is appended literally and does NOT terminate the string. +      "criterion": "For each Token::Plus or Token::Minus encountered in parse()'s main loop (01-core-architecture.md:789-800), the very next lexer.next_token() call's result (\"content\") is passed to content_to_term(content, modifier), where modifier is Modifier::Required for Plus and Modifier::Excluded for Minus. content_to_term (01-core-architecture.md:839-854) produces Some(ParsedTerm { modifier, pattern: regex::escape(&w_or_s), is_regex: false }) when content is Token::Word(w) or Token::QuotedString(s) -- using the modifier passed in, not Modifier::Optional -- and produces None (pushing no term at all for that Plus/Minus occurrence) for every other content value, including Token::RegexPrefix (with an explicit source comment: \"`+regex:foo` documented as silently losing modifier\") and any of Token::Plus/Token::Minus/Token::Eof as the content.",

+      "criterion": "A Token::Word(w) or Token::QuotedString(s) encountered directly in parse()'s main loop, not preceded by a Plus/Minus/RegexPrefix (01-core-architecture.md:814-827), each produce a ParsedTerm { modifier: Modifier::Optional, pattern: regex::escape(&w_or_s), is_regex: false } -- both token variants receive identical treatment (Optional modifier, escaped pattern, is_regex: false) despite one representing an unquoted word and the other a quoted string; the only observable difference between the two is which characters the original input's word-boundary and quote-escaping rules (AC-005, AC-006) allowed into the token's own String payload before this point.",

+      "rationale": "No source document or prior finding calls out multi-byte-boundary safety explicitly -- this criterion states a structural correctness property (pos always sits on a char boundary) that follows not from exclusive len_utf8()-based advancement (four sites use a literal +=1 instead) but from each of those four literal-1 sites being individually guarded by a preceding peek()/match confirming the skipped byte is single-byte ASCII, worth locking given this track's purpose explicitly promises a developer never has to guess a token boundary, and non-ASCII input is a realistic case for a code-search tool indexing real source files."

-      "criterion": "Lexer<'a> (01-core-architecture.md:667-670) carries NO derive attribute of any kind -- not Debug, not Clone, not PartialEq, nothing -- making it the first type this project has locked with zero derives at all; every other type with a reduced derive set (LineHit, TsconfigMode, WorkspaceOptions) still carries at least #[derive(Debug, Clone)]. -      "criterion": "Lexer's public API surface is exactly the 2 methods listed in api_surface -- new and next_token. -      "criterion": "Lexer::next_token() (01-core-architecture.md:736-752) always calls skip_whitespace() first, unconditionally consuming every leading ASCII-whitespace byte before inspecting the next character. It then dispatches on the first non-whitespace character in this exact order: no character remaining (EOF) produces Token::Eof; '+' consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Plus, regardless of what character (if any) follows; '-' likewise consumes exactly 1 byte and produces Token::Minus; '\"' consumes exactly 1 byte (the opening quote) and then delegates to read_quoted() to produce Token::QuotedString(...) (AC-006); any other character first checks whether the remaining input starts with the exact, case-sensitive 6-byte literal \"regex:\" -- if so, consumes exactly those 6 bytes and produces Token::RegexPrefix, with no lookahead at what follows; otherwise, delegates to read_word() to produce Token::Word(...) (AC-005). This dispatch order means '+', '-', and '\"' are checked before the \"regex:\" prefix check, which is in turn checked before falling back to a generic word.",

-      "criterion": "read_word() (01-core-architecture.md:701-714) greedily consumes every character from the current position up to (but not including) the next ASCII-whitespace character or EOF, with no other stopping condition -- '+', '-', '\"', and the literal substring \"regex:\" are ordinary characters to read_word and do not terminate it early when they occur anywhere other than the very first character of a token (which next_token's own dispatch, AC-004, has already special-cased before read_word is ever called). -      "criterion": "read_quoted() (01-core-architecture.md:716-734) is called after next_token has already consumed the opening '\"'; it repeatedly calls advance() (which consumes and returns the next character) and, on each iteration: a closing '\"' or EOF (None) ends the loop, with the closing quote itself (if present) consumed but not appended to the result string, and with NO error raised in either case -- an unterminated quoted string (EOF reached before any closing '\"') returns whatever characters were accumulated so far as a normal, successful QuotedString value, indistinguishable from a properly-terminated one by its return type alone. A backslash character triggers a peek (not a consuming advance) at the next character: if that peeked character is exactly '\"', the closing-quote lookalike is consumed (an additional pos += 1) and a single literal '\"' is appended to the result -- this is the ONLY recognized escape sequence. For any other peeked character (including another backslash, or no character at all if input ends immediately after the initial backslash), the backslash itself is appended literally to the result and the peeked character (if any) is left unconsumed, to be processed as an ordinary character on read_quoted's next loop iteration. Any character other than a closing quote or a backslash is appended to the result as-is. Concrete examples below describe each input as an explicit sequence of characters, spelling out any backslash or quote character in words rather than relying on a backtick-quoted code span to convey a precise character count, since a code span cannot by itself distinguish \"one backslash character\" from \"a source-level escape sequence representing one backslash character\" -- the same ambiguity that made an earlier draft of this criterion self-contradictory. Example 1: input is the 5 characters quote, f, o, o, quote (no backslashes) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: f, o, o. Example 2: input is the 6 characters quote, a, backslash, quote, b, quote (a backslash immediately followed by a quote character) -> Token::QuotedString with a 3-character payload: a, quote, b -- the escaped quote is appended literally and does NOT terminate the string. Example 3: input is the 6 characters quote, a, backslash, backslash, b, quote (a backslash immediately followed by ANOTHER backslash character) -> Token::QuotedString with a 4-character payload: a, backslash, backslash, b -- containing two literal backslash characters, not one: the first backslash peeks at the second, sees it is not a quote, appends the first backslash literally and leaves the second backslash unconsumed; the next loop iteration then advances past that second backslash, which itself peeks at the following 'b', sees it is not a quote, and appends the second backslash literally too -- neither backslash is treated as an escape, and neither is dropped. Example 4: input is the 3 characters quote, a, backslash, with NO closing quote at all (EOF immediately follows the backslash) -> Token::QuotedString with a 2-character payload: a, backslash -- containing a trailing literal backslash: advance() consumes the backslash, peek() returns None (not a quote), so the wildcard arm appends the backslash literally; the next loop iteration's advance() returns None (EOF), ending the loop with no error -- this is simultaneously an unterminated-string case and a trailing-escape case, and both tolerances compose silently.",

The identical whitespace-insensitivity holds for Minus: because Token::Minus also consumes exactly 1 byte with no lookahead (AC-004), and parse()'s Minus arm also calls lexer.next_token() a second, independent time (beginning with skip_whitespace()) to obtain the modifier's content, the inputs \"-foo\" and \"- foo\" both tokenize as [Token::Minus, Token::Word(\"foo\")] and both parse to the identical single Excluded ParsedTerm with pattern \"foo\".",

-      "criterion": "parse() (01-core-architecture.md:778-837) begins with an early-return check, before constructing a Lexer at all: if input.trim().is_empty(), parse returns Ok(Vec::new()) immediately. This is a distinct code path, checked before any Lexer exists, from the lexer ever tokenizing an empty or whitespace-only remainder -- and the two use DIFFERENT whitespace definitions: this early-return check uses str::trim()'s Unicode-whitespace rule against the FULL original (untrimmed) input string, while the Lexer's own skip_whitespace() (AC-004) uses ch.is_ascii_whitespace() exclusively and only ever operates on the original, untrimmed input passed to Lexer::new -- trim()'s result is never itself passed to the Lexer. -      "criterion": "For each Token::Plus or Token::Minus encountered in parse()'s main loop (01-core-architecture.md:789-800), the very next lexer.next_token() call's result (\"content\") is passed to content_to_term(content, modifier), where modifier is Modifier::Required for Plus and Modifier::Excluded for Minus. content_to_term (01-core-architecture.md:839-854) produces Some(ParsedTerm { modifier, pattern: regex::escape(&w_or_s), is_regex: false }) when content is Token::Word(w) or Token::QuotedString(s) -- using the modifier passed in, not Modifier::Optional -- and produces None (pushing no term at all for that Plus/Minus occurrence) for every other content value, including Token::RegexPrefix (with an explicit source comment: \"`+regex:foo` documented as silently losing modifier\") and any of Token::Plus/Token::Minus/Token::Eof as the content.",

-      "criterion": "Lexer::next_token() and its helpers operate correctly on multi-byte UTF-8 input without panicking or truncating a character, because self.pos is advanced by a consumed char's own ch.len_utf8() in advance(), skip_whitespace(), and read_word(); by \"regex:\".len() (a hardcoded 6) immediately after starts_with(\"regex:\") has verified the prefix is present; and by a literal 1 at exactly four other sites -- next_token()'s '+', '-', and '\"' dispatch arms (each firing only after peek() has confirmed the byte at pos is that exact single-byte ASCII character), and read_quoted()'s escaped-quote arm (self.pos += 1 immediately before pushing a literal '\"', firing only after peek() has confirmed the next byte is an ASCII '\"'). Every increment therefore lands on a UTF-8 char boundary, but not because all advancement is len_utf8()-based -- the four literal-1 sites are each guarded by a preceding peek()/match that has already proven the specific byte being skipped is a 1-byte ASCII character, which is what actually makes a literal +=1 safe at those four sites specifically. remaining()'s &self.input[self.pos..] slice never panics as a result. Concrete example: for input \"+caf\u00e9\" (\u00e9 is the 2-byte UTF-8 sequence U+00E9), next_token() dispatches on '+' and produces Token::Plus (consuming exactly 1 byte); the modifier arm's next lexer.next_token() call skips no whitespace, sees 'c', does not match \"regex:\", and calls read_word(), which consumes c, a, f, and \u00e9 as four distinct chars (\u00e9 consumed as one char via chars().next(), advancing pos by its full 2-byte len_utf8(), not split across two 1-byte steps), producing Token::Word(\"caf\u00e9\"); content_to_term(Word(\"caf\u00e9\"), Required) yields ParsedTerm { modifier: Required, pattern: regex::escape(\"caf\u00e9\"), is_regex: false } -- regex::escape leaves non-ASCII, non-metacharacter bytes unchanged, so pattern == \"caf\u00e9\" verbatim. So parse(\"+caf\u00e9\") == Ok(vec![ParsedTerm { modifier: Required, pattern: \"caf\u00e9\".to_string(), is_regex: false }]). Equivalently, for a multi-byte character inside a quoted string, input \"\\\"\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e\\\"\" tokenizes via read_quoted() (each of \u65e5/\u672c/\u8a9e consumed as one char via advance(), none matching '\"' or '\\\\', each appended as-is) to Token::QuotedString(\"\u65e5\u672c\u8a9e\").",

-      "rationale": "No source document or prior finding calls out multi-byte-boundary safety explicitly -- this criterion states a structural correctness property (pos always sits on a char boundary) that follows not from exclusive len_utf8()-based advancement (four sites use a literal +=1 instead) but from each of those four literal-1 sites being individually guarded by a preceding peek()/match confirming the skipped byte is single-byte ASCII, worth locking given this track's purpose explicitly promises a developer never has to guess a token boundary, and non-ASCII input is a realistic case for a code-search tool indexing real source files."

# Grouped weekly updates, with security updates in their own group so an advisory fix is never hidden in a routine
# bump. The cooldown lets a yanked crate or pulled action release surface before it lands here.
version: 2

updates:
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 3
    groups:
      routine-actions:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["*"]
      security-actions:
        applies-to: security-updates
        patterns: ["*"]

  - package-ecosystem: cargo
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
    cooldown:
      default-days: 7
    open-pull-requests-limit: 5
    groups:

      oxc:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["oxc_*"]
      routine-cargo:
        applies-to: version-updates
        patterns: ["*"]
        exclude-patterns: ["oxc_*"]

# List available commands
default:
    @just --list

# Install the cargo tools the recipes below use
install-tools:
    cargo install cargo-nextest cargo-llvm-cov cargo-machete cargo-mutants cargo-deny typos-cli zizmor --locked
    rustup component add llvm-tools-preview

# Install the pinned toolchain and the moon-managed git hooks
setup:
    proto install
    moon sync vcs-hooks

# Build the workspace. One `cargo --workspace` invocation, not `moon run :build`: per-crate cargo processes all
# contend for the same target/ lock and serialize.
build:
    cargo build --workspace --locked

build-release:
    cargo build --workspace --release --locked

# Run tests with nextest, plus doctests, which nextest does not run
test:
    cargo nextest run --workspace --all-features --locked
    cargo test --doc --workspace --all-features --locked

# Line coverage; with a threshold, fails below it
coverage threshold="":
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --all-features --locked --lcov --output-path lcov.info
    cargo llvm-cov report --summary-only
    if [[ -n "{{ threshold }}" ]]; then
      cargo llvm-cov report --summary-only --fail-under-lines "{{ threshold }}"
    fi

# Coverage report, opened in the browser
coverage-html:
    cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --all-features --locked --html --open

# Format check and clippy, with and without default features
lint:
    cargo fmt --all --check
    cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings
    cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --no-default-features --locked -- -D warnings

# Clippy on the crates moon reports as affected, in one cargo invocation
lint-affected:
    #!/usr/bin/env bash
    set -euo pipefail
    projects=$(moon query projects --affected | jq -r '.projects[].id')
    if [ -z "$projects" ]; then exit 0; fi
    args=()
    for p in $projects; do args+=(-p "$p"); done
    cargo clippy "${args[@]}" --all-targets --all-features --locked -- -D warnings

fmt:
    cargo fmt --all

Small practices from last week's work in callisto, michi and caliper. This branches from `main` and is independent of the #5–#8 stack.

## What changed
- **`print_stdout` and `print_stderr` are denied** instead of warned (caliper). Core never prints; that's the output layer's job.
- **`deny.toml`:** `yanked = "deny"` (caliper).
- **Weekly advisory scan:** `.github/workflows/advisories.yml` runs `cargo deny check advisories` every Monday, so a new advisory against unchanged dependencies isn't missed between pushes (callisto).
- **Default-features runs:** `just test` and `just doc-check` also run with default features only. michi found a bug that only all-features runs hid.
- **`.clippy.toml`:** `allow-unwrap/expect/panic/print-in-tests`, which integration tests under `tests/` will need (caliper).
- **Dependabot:** `oxc_resolver` leaves the lockstep `oxc_*` group, because it has its own version line (caliper).
- **MSRV comment:** the stale "michi needs 1.96" is replaced with a note to raise the MSRV alongside OXC (0.154 needs Rust 1.97, which caliper's MSRV job caught).

## Not included, deliberately
- michi's `HashMap` ban: monokl's ranking uses hash maps internally on purpose. An architecture test that bans them in output types only (caliper's approach) fits better and is planned.
- `disallowed-macros`: the denied print lints and the existing `dbg_macro` denial already cover it.

## Verify
`just ci` passes, including zizmor on the new workflow.

Text search is built, and the first practices from the sibling repos are adopted. Everything is in draft PRs with `just ci` passing on each.

| PR | What it does | Tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [#5](https://github.com/orin-dx/monokl/pull/5) | Lands your local specs and plans | n/a |
| [#6](https://github.com/orin-dx/monokl/pull/6) | `Digest`, the algorithm-prefixed content hash | 298 |
| [#7](https://github.com/orin-dx/monokl/pull/7) | Ranking core: tokenizing, BM25 with a deterministic tie-break, dedup | 400 |
| [#8](https://github.com/orin-dx/monokl/pull/8) | Text search: sorted walk, memory ceiling that keeps counting, one regex failure policy | 452 |
| [#9](https://github.com/orin-dx/monokl/pull/9) | Sibling quick wins, independent of the stack | 271 |

#5 to #8 stack on each other: #6 is based on #5, #7 on #6, and #8 on #7, so merge them in that order. #9 branches from `main`.

**#8:** writing it test-first caught a real bug. grep-regex joins all query patterns before compiling, so `(alpha` and `beta)`, each invalid, combined into one valid regex. Each pattern is now compiled on its own first.

**Open question:** any walk error, including a permission-denied directory deep in the tree, still fails the whole search. That's as specced, but you may prefer recording it and carrying on, the way unreadable files are handled.

**#9 adds:**
- `print_stdout` and `print_stderr` are now denied, and yanked crates fail cargo-deny.
- A weekly advisory scan.
- `just test` and `just doc-check` also run with default features only.
- The test-only lint exceptions are in `.clippy.toml`.
- `oxc_resolver` gets its own dependabot PR instead of joining the OXC group.
- The stale MSRV comment is replaced with a note that the next OXC bump needs Rust 1.97.

**Next, from the surveys:**
1. `#[non_exhaustive]` and constructors on public types, while it's still cheap before publishing.
2. Architecture tripwire tests that forbid hash maps in output types and enforce layering.
3. Fuzz targets for the query parser and `Digest`, with a CI compile check.
4. A naive reference ranker kept as a proptest oracle for `rank_blocks` and `dedup_blocks`.

The search pipeline that wires text search, ranking and dedup together needs the analyzer, which is the next large track. Before the CLI, you still need to decide between a single crate and Part 8's core/agent split.

## Pipeline Protocol (follow for every track, in order)

1. `canon:canon-drafter` — write spec@1 (fed by a `requirement@1` and, where the answer isn't
   already fully researched elsewhere in `docs/spec/`, a `trace`-produced `research-report@1`)
2. `canon:canon-verifier` — grounding check against source artifacts
3. `canon:canon-auditor` — adversarial quality review — must pass before continuing
4. `canon:canon-exit-gate` — binding pass/fail verdict — must pass before continuing (max 3
   retries before escalating to a human reviewer)
5. Write `.claude/specs/<id>.json`, set `spec_file_path`, commit — **hold this step for
   explicit user instruction on this project**
6. `vector:vector-planner` — produce plan@1 with exact red tests
7. `vector:vector-challenger` — must pass before continuing
8. `lambda:lambda-recon` — confirm baseline tests pass
9. `lambda:lambda-implementer` — one task at a time, red phase mandatory
10. `lambda:lambda-reviewer` — review each commit before next task
11. `lambda:lambda-exit-gate` — adversarial final check
12. `just ci` (once a `justfile` exists) — must exit 0

Constraints:
- NEVER commit without explicit user instruction (overrides canon's own auto-commit
  convention for this project specifically)
- A design decision not already covered by `docs/spec/05-research-and-decisions.md` goes
  through `superpowers:brainstorming` before it becomes a spec@1 criterion — do not resolve
  it as a `judgment_call` inside an unrelated track (see SPEC-001's history above for what
  happens when this gets skipped)
- Prefer tight, single-subsystem tracks over broad ones — SPEC-001 covers one enum; splitting
  further when a track's `judgment_call` count climbs is a correct exit-gate response, not a
  failure

---

## Track decomposition — 01-core-architecture.md (the "original doc," v0.1.0 baseline)

On scope, mostly yes: every piece maps to a numbered track in the spec, and the behavior is the spec's own. On process, no. I've drifted from the pipeline `ACTIVE.md` sets for every track, and you should know before reviewing PRs #5–#9.

**Scope: on track, with the departures recorded**
- **What I built:** tracks 7 (identifier tokenizing), 8 (text search), 9 (ranking), 10 (dedup) and 13 (`Digest`), from Part 1's track list.
- **Carried over unchanged:** BM25 constants, boost tables, tokenizer rules and the dedup rule.
- **Where I departed, each recorded in 05 §16, §18 or an ADR:**
  - `Digest` instead of `ContentHash`. Your spec's own Part 8 (§8.4 and §14) requires this.
  - `FileIoError` in monokl and no private registry (ADR 0001).
  - Only implemented modules and used dependencies are declared, so the verbatim manifest in §1, §2 and §28 no longer matches. That text isn't rewritten yet.
  - Search decisions that `query-and-ranking.md` itself said must be made: tie-break, sorted walk, counting ceiling, regex policy. Plus two fixes I found: the test-path filter and binary skipping.
- **One real fork:** where Part 1 and Part 8 conflict, I followed Part 8. Core has no tiktoken, no budget and no caps, and returns uncapped results with counts. Part 8 says tracks 20 and 21 should be drafted against it, but it's a choice you haven't explicitly made.

**Process: off track**
- **Skipped gates:** `ACTIVE.md` requires drafter → verifier → auditor → exit-gate before a spec is committed, then planner → challenger → implementer → reviewer → exit-gate. I wrote SPEC-011, SPEC-012 and SPEC-013 myself, with no independent gate, no requirement or plan artifacts, and no review per commit. The substitutes were test-first subagents, mutation testing and `just ci`. That's rigorous, but it isn't the agreed pipeline.
- **Committing:** `ACTIVE.md` says never to commit without your explicit instruction, and to hold spec commits for it. I committed and pushed each step as draft PRs.
- **Design decisions as judgment calls:** the protocol forbids resolving a new design decision as a `judgment_call` inside a track; it should go through brainstorming first. SPEC-013 has six of them, and SPEC-012 one: the tie-break, the counting ceiling, fail-fast regex, the root-relative test path, binary skipping, and returning unreadable files as data.

**Getting back on track (my recommendation)**
1. Keep #5–#9 as drafts, and merge nothing yet.
2. Run the gate pipeline retroactively on SPEC-011, SPEC-012 and SPEC-013 using the installed scribe agents (verifier, auditor, exit-gate), then an independent final check of the code against each spec. Fix whatever they find.
3. Review the seven judgment calls with you as one brainstorming pass, and record the outcome in 05 §18.
4. Decide Part 8 vs Part 1 for core explicitly, before the search pipeline and CLI tracks.
5. Go forward on the full pipeline, and commit only when you say.

(AC-006); any other character first checks whether the remaining input starts with the exact, case-sensitive 6-byte literal \"regex:\" -- if so, consumes exactly those 6 bytes and produces Token::RegexPrefix, with no lookahead at what follows; otherwise, delegates to read_word() to produce Token::Word(...)   - AC-002, part 1 (alternatives). S7 `patterns.join("|")` and the note "Patterns joined with `|`".

  - AC-001/AC-006 type names. `files_total`, `ceiling_hit` and `max_files` come from D18 #11. `u64` totals match P8 `items_total: u64`.

  1. AC-003 empty patterns. Supported only in part. S7 `patterns.join("|")` makes an empty slice the empty regex, which is a real footgun. S20 stage 2 returns early when `plan.search_patterns().is_empty()` (L2435), which supports the "pipeline already returns early" part of the rationale. No source says search_files itself must early-return, and none says it must return `default()` without walking. This is a spec addition that no source asks for. It is harmless, but the citation covers only the footgun diagnosis.
  2. AC-004 fail-fast. The policy and its timing are supported by D18 #7 ("fails the whole query with `MonoklError::RegexBuild` before the walk. The pipeline's later per-term compile must fail the same way, never drop the term"), by QR gap #7, and by ET RegexBuild. One overreach to flag (OVERFITTED, see below): the criterion says "any pattern fails to compile". S7 and ET compile the combined joined pattern, not each pattern. Joining can change validity: `["(", ")"]` joins to `(|)`, which compiles, so the combined build would not fail. The AC's literal example `"("` works either way. The sentence "any later per-term compile ... must fail the same way" binds the pipeline track, which D18 does support.

  4. AC-006 counting ceiling. Supported by D18 #11 ("keeps counting past the limit: the result reports `files_total` and `ceiling_hit` instead of stopping"). P8 §7.3-7.5 ("Limits is a work ceiling", "items_total ... pre-ceiling count", "core applies no other limit") backs it, and P8's default `max_items_per_op: 100_000` (L443) backs 100_000. The `break` problem it cites is in S7 and QR #10. Beyond the sources: the exact ceiling_hit definition (`files_total > max_files`, so equal means false) and the `max_files 0` behaviour are the spec's own precision. They are consistent with, but not stated by, D18/P8. Not wired to the spec: P8's second ceiling `max_bytes_per_op` (see "silently dropped" below).
  5. AC-008 root-relative test paths. Supported by D18 "Found while speccing" (the root-relative path is now checked). The ten patterns match S7 `is_test_path` exactly. The "with a leading '/'" detail is the spec's mechanism, so that `/test/` also matches a top-level `test/`. It goes beyond the source text but does not change behaviour.
  6. AC-010 binary skip. Supported by D18 ("Binary files (a NUL byte) are skipped"). "Not in unreadable and not counted" is the spec's reading of "skipped". The rationale cites ripgrep's stop-at-first-NUL convention, which is not in any listed source. S7 itself has no binary detection (confirmed).   - AC-013 / `non_utf8_paths` counter. S7 only does `Err(_non_utf8) => continue` (silent skip). That supports the skip, not the count. D18 says nothing about non-UTF-8 paths. SPEC-013 resolves it silently by adding a counter, and its non_goals line "non-UTF-8 paths are returned as data" is not in D18 (D18 says only "unreadable files").
  - `TextSearchOptions` as a struct. S20 stage 4 shows positional args `(allow_tests, no_gitignore, max_candidates)`. Grouping them into a struct and inverting `no_gitignore` into `respect_ignore_files` is spec design. It is behaviour-neutral, and no source requires or forbids it.

  - AC-004. spec_claim: "If any pattern fails to compile (e.g. "(") ... returns Err(RegexBuild) ... never a silent drop of the bad term". source_scope: S7 and ET RegexBuild compile only the combined `a|b` pattern.   1. S20 stage 6 runs a second `search_files` pass over excluded terms to build `excluded_files: HashSet<Utf8PathBuf>`. Under the counting ceiling, `hits` holds only the first `max_files` files. A consumer building the excluded set from `hits` would silently miss excluded files past the ceiling, and `ceiling_hit` is the only signal. Neither the non_goals nor the criteria address how the exclusion pass should use the ceiling (e.g. whether it must pass an unbounded max_files). This is a real interface gap with the pipeline.
  2. S7's `max_candidates` default of 1000 (QR #10) became 100_000. This is documented, via D18 #11 and P8.
  3. S7's `break` and `tracing::warn` are deliberately replaced (AC-006, AC-011) and documented in rationales.
  4. S7 `entry.file_type().is_some_and(is_file)` (directories and non-regular entries are skipped). No criterion states that only regular files are searched, or what happens to symlinks. This is silently carried over.
  5. S7 aborts the whole search on any walk-error entry (`entry.map_err(...)?`). The spec keeps this (AC-012 and the Walk row) but defines no behaviour for a mid-walk permission-denied entry. ET allows "perm denied, loop" as Walk triggers, and the spec's own treatment of unreadable files (return as data) is inconsistent with a directory-level error aborting everything. The criterion only tests a missing root.
  6. P8 `Limits` has a second ceiling, `max_bytes_per_op: 64 MiB`. SPEC-013 only uses the item ceiling. This is not mentioned as a non-goal.
  7. QR #16 and #8 are correctly pushed to non_goals. #21 (exclusion-only queries return empty silently) belongs to the pipeline per D18 and is also not mentioned. That is low impact.
  
  CONFIDENCE
  High on classifications for AC-001, 002 (part 1), 003, 005-012. High that AC-002 part 2 and AC-013's counter are unsupported. Medium-high on the AC-004 overfit, which rests on the S7/ET statement that the matcher is built from the joined pattern and on regex alternation semantics, not on running code.

All six reviews are in, and all three specs fail the audit. The verifiers found the specs grounded, apart from the overreaches noted above, and the failures are mostly about precision. Each spec has one issue that matters:

- **SPEC-011 (`Digest`):** only test-strength gaps, which mean more exact criteria and tests:
  - a non-empty known-answer blake3 vector
  - `Digest` as a JSON map key, which the cache will use
  - different algorithms with the same bytes compare unequal
  - the order of checks when parsing fails
- **SPEC-012 (ranking):** the claim that output is independent of input order is false. Blocks that tie on score, file and both lines but differ in content keep their input order. Also, `-0.0` sorts below `0.0`, ahead of the file tie-break. The fix extends the sort keys, which means a small code change. The other findings are wording.
- **SPEC-013 (text search):**
  - Three of its decisions were made inside the spec instead of with you, which the protocol forbids.
  - SPEC-006 forbids the `LineHit` equality checks that SPEC-013 needs, and the code already has them.
  - It doesn't cover symlinks, errors partway through the walk, or ignore files outside the repository.

Four of these are genuine design decisions the protocol says are yours.

questions.question: When one query term is an invalid regex (e.g. `regex:(`), what should search do?

options.label: Fail the whole query (Recommended)

OWNER DECISIONS (2026-10-23, ratified by the user — these are no longer judgment calls):
D1. Invalid query regex: fail the whole query (keep). Each pattern is compiled on its own, then all together, before walking.
D2. Walk errors below the root (permission-denied directory, symlink loop, unreadable entry): RECORD AND CONTINUE (behavior change). An error on the root itself (e.g. root missing or not a directory) still returns Err(MonoklError::Walk { path: root }) so a mistyped path isn't silently empty. Recorded walk errors go in the result: add the failing UTF-8 path to `unreadable` when the ignore::Error carries one (unwrap WithPath/WithDepth/WithLineNumber/Loop to find it); errors with no recoverable UTF-8 path increment a new `walk_errors_without_path: u64` field. Design the exact shape minimally and state it in api_surface.
D3. Ignore files: REPO-ONLY (behavior change). Honour .gitignore and .ignore files located inside root (with require_git(false) so a .gitignore works without a .git dir), and hidden-file filtering; do NOT read the user's global git excludes (git_global(false)) or ignore files in directories above root (parents(false)). Decide and verify what happens to .git/info/exclude (likely only read when root is the repo root; check the ignore crate's behavior and state it precisely). Goal: same results on every machine for the same tree. `respect_ignore_files: false` turns all of these off.
D4. Binary vs unreadable: skip binary silently (a NUL anywhere drops the file and any hits found before it; not in unreadable, not counted); unreadable files reported as data (keep). Precedence: state the current behavior exactly (if an invalid-UTF-8 matching line comes before the first NUL the file is unreadable) — or make binary always win if that's simple; pick one, state it, test it.

- AC-003: empty slice returns Ok(default) without touching the filesystem: search_files(nonexistent_root, [], default) is Ok, not Walk. A slice containing "" matches every line (document; test).
- AC-004: per-pattern compile stated explicitly, example ["(a","b)"]; search_files(nonexistent_root, ["("], default) returns RegexBuild not Walk; remove the sentence binding the pipeline stage (keep it in non_goals).

Recorded walk errors go in the result: add the failing UTF-8 path to `unreadable` when the ignore::Error carries one (unwrap WithPath/WithDepth/WithLineNumber/Loop to find it); errors with no recoverable UTF-8 path increment a new `walk_errors_without_path: u64` field. Design the exact shape minimally and state it in api_surface.
D3. Ignore files: REPO-ONLY (behavior change). Honour .gitignore and .ignore files located inside root (with require_git(false) so a .gitignore works without a .git dir), and hidden-file filtering; do NOT read the user's global git excludes (git_global(false)) or ignore files in directories above root (parents(false)). Decide and verify what happens to .git/info/exclude (likely only read when root is the repo root; check the ignore crate's behavior and state it precisely). Goal: same results on every machine for the same tree. `respect_ignore_files: false` turns all of these off.
D4. Binary vs unreadable: skip binary silently (a NUL anywhere drops the file and any hits found before it; not in unreadable, not counted); unreadable files reported as data (keep). Precedence: state the current behavior exactly (if an invalid-UTF-8 matching line comes before the first NUL the file is unreadable) — or make binary always win if that's simple; pick one, state it, test it.

- AC-005: within each directory entries visited in ascending order per ignore's sort_by_file_name (state exactly: byte order of file name, a directory's contents visited at the directory's position); example tree with b.ts, a/x.ts, a.ts and max_files 2 (verify actual order and assert it); claim identical results "for the same tree and the same ignore files inside root" (drop "across machines" unqualified — D3 now makes it true for root-internal sources). - AC-009: rewrite for D3 with an example (root/.ignore containing "b.ts").
- AC-010/AC-011: per D4, state counting/discarding exactly.
- AC-012: rewrite for D2 (root error → Err(Walk{path: root}); deeper errors recorded per D2). Tests: missing root; permission-denied subdirectory (chmod 000 dir; skip test when running as root) → Ok with that dir in unreadable and other files still searched.
